http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/31/alger.text: Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune is seeking to reinstate the death penalty for arsonists following deadly wildfires that have ravaged parts of the country.Tebboune declared three days of national mourning on Thursday after wildfires in the northeast of the country killed at least 12 people and injured dozens more.In a statement, Tebboune described the loss of life as "a great tragedy," as officials maintained the official death toll from Wednesday.Algeria has observed a moratorium on the death penalty since 1993, but the Algerian head of state has ordered that "an amendment to the Criminal Code" be made by 15 September.12 people died, 54 in hospitalInterior Minister Saïd Sayoud confirmed five fatalities in Jijel province, four in Béjaïa, and three in Tizi Ouzou following the outbreak of the fires. He added that 54 people were receiving hospital treatment for burns, six of whom remain in critical condition.Algeria’s civil protection agency reported on Thursday morning that 46 fires remained active out of 193 recorded over the previous 24 hours. Unverified videos shared online overnight depicted sweeping blazes trapping residents in their homes.The national gendarmerie announced that three major highways linking eastern regions were closed due to forest fires raging near Béjaïa, Jijel and Sétif.While summer forest fires occur regularly in northern Algeria, more frequent droughts and extreme heat have been adding to their intensity. In July 2023, fires swept through thousands of hectares of forest and farmland near Béjaïa, destroying hundreds of homes and leaving more than 30 people dead. Authorities recorded nearly 2,000 fires nationwide in July this year alone.

The US president has said he is working on a deal to buy fertiliser from Belarus, pivoting away from main supplier Canada. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters Belarus Trump seeks ‘massive’ Belarus fertiliser deal amid Canada trade war Trump’s announcement on Russia ally comes as he steps up his trade war with Canada, a long-term US ally and top supplier of potash Agence France-Presse Tue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google President Donald Trump has said he is working on a “massive” deal to buy fertiliser from Belarus , pivoting away from main supplier Canada amid an escalating trade dispute, and moving instead toward an ally of Russia. “The United States is working on a massive deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada , very good news for our farmers and ranchers.” In recent weeks Trump has stepped up his trade war with Canada , a long-term US ally and the country’s biggest supplier of potash. Whiplashed middle powers seek new alliances as Trump rages on world stage Read more The announcement on Monday shows Washington’s willingness to pursue dialogue with Minsk despite its repression of dissidents and support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The US imports most of its potash – a chemical salt used to manufacture fertiliser – and prices soared after the Ukraine war began in 2022. In 2024, 79% came from Canada, 11% from Russia and 4% from Belarus, according to the US Geological Survey. Washington has quietly moved to thaw relations with Belarus under Trump’s second administration. Last week, Belarus freed 25 political prisoners as the US lifted sanctions on two of the country’s companies. But hundreds remain in prison after President Alexander Lukashenko, in power since 1994, suppressed mass protests over his reelection in 2020 , which was followed by a wave of sanctions. Western countries again squeezed Belarus with sanctions in 2022 after Minsk allowed Moscow to invade Ukraine through its territory. Belarus’s exiled opposition leader, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, on Monday warned that any deal with Lukashenko was “very risky”. “Our position is that it is not time to trade with the regime while all the income from potash goes to repression, goes to support of the Russian war machine,” Tsikhanouskaya told Agence France-Presse. She stressed, however, her belief that Americans “know who Lukashenko is”. https://krcgtv.com/news/local/17-year-ol.text: A 17-year-old Warsaw girl was injured in a crash Saturday evening in Benton County. According to the Missouri State Highway Patrol (MSHP), the crash happened around 6:33 p.m. Saturday, October 3, on US-65 south of Missouri 7. Troopers say the 17-year-old was driving a 1997 GMC Sierra southbound when she changed lanes and clipped a 2005 Chevrolet Silverado, also traveling southbound and driven by a 19-year-old Lincoln man. After the initial contact, the GMC crossed the highway, ran off the left side of the road, struck a Missouri Department of Transportation sign and overturned. The 17-year-old suffered moderate injuries and was taken by Warsaw/Lincoln EMS to Golden Valley Memorial Hospital for treatment. The report lists her safety device use as unknown. The 19-year-old driver of the Silverado was not injured. His vehicle sustained moderate damage and was towed from the scene by a family member. .The GMC was totaled and towed from the scene by Twin Lakes

https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/opinion.text: LETTER TO THE EDITOR Why a stronger Europe matters to Asia’s security It may spare an already-stretched America entanglements in a second theatre Summarise Share Add to Preferred Sources Add to Preferred Sources Published Thu, Nov 5, 2026 · 07:00 AM In 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, and in September 2025 its drones crossed into Poland, prompting Warsaw to invoke Nato’s Article 4. PHOTO: REUTERS I REFER to Mohan Kuppusamy’s commentary, “ If Europe goes to war, the fallout will be felt in East Asia ” (Oct 15, 2026). He is right that a Nato-Russia war would be ruinous for Asia’s trade-dependent economies, and that preparing for war is not the same as preventing it. I would add three points on where the danger lies. First, an under-armed Europe is the likelier invitation to attack. Europe is not rearming because Russia is stronger, but Russia is close, heavily armed, and perceived in European capitals to have hostile intent. In 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, and in September 2025 its drones crossed into Poland, prompting Warsaw to invoke Nato’s Article 4. In June 2026, Germany’s army chief said Nato members agree Russia could launch a large-scale assault on allied territory before the end of the decade. Kuppusamy seems to read Germany’s goal of a “war-ready” Bundeswehr by 2029 as fatalism, but Danish defence intelligence assesses Russia could be ready for large-scale war within five years if it perceives Nato as weak or divided. THE BUSINESS TIMES INSIGHTS Powering Asean's Future 2026 Find out how enterprises are navigating power constraints and sustainability targets ACCESS THE INSIGHTS Second, Europe cannot count on Washington to fill the gap. The 2026 US National Defense Strategy asks Nato allies to take “primary responsibility for Europe’s conventional defence”. America is already stretched. Since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February 2026, hundreds of air defence interceptors have moved from South Korea and elsewhere in Asia to the Middle East. Europe’s 29 Nato members spent 487 billion euros (US$559 billion) on defence in 2025, and this is expected to grow to about US$639 billion in 2026. Meanwhile, Russia reportedly plans to spend US$202.58 billion on defence in 2027. SEE ALSO If Europe goes to war, the fallout will be felt in East Asia Russia is the test of Europe’s strategic autonomy Are Europe and America headed for divorce? Third, if Europe does stumble into war, it would likelier be through what it acquires than how much it spends. Here, Kuppusamy’s caution is well justified. The security dilemma is sharpest when defensive and offensive weapons cannot be told apart. Air defence, minefields and border fortifications raise the cost of invasion without threatening Russian territory; long-range strike weapons threaten it directly. Europe is moving towards the latter. After Washington appeared to shelve plans to station long-range missiles in Germany, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in July 2026 that Germany would buy Tomahawk cruise missiles itself. Moscow treats such weapons as provocative, as its August 2025 exit from a moratorium on intermediate-range missiles showed. Germany has also ordered 536 million euros of artificial intelligence-guided strike drones, first for its brigade in Lithuania. Such systems speed up how fast a military can observe, decide and act. That helps a defender, but also cuts the time that states need to judge each other’s intent. Combined with Russia’s 2024 doctrine lowering its nuclear threshold, this is one way Europe could compress the path to war. Europe should therefore weight its rearmament towards defence. A Europe that can defend itself may not pull America out of the Middle East, nor guarantee that Washington stays committed to its long-term interests in Asia. Yet it may spare an already-stretched America entanglements in a second theatre, and leave it the wherewithal to preserve Asia’s balance of power.
